headline: Older Cochrane pregnancy review flags high-protein supplementation as no-benefit and potentially harmful.
implication: Pregnancy should be a protocol safety exclusion or clinician-guidance path, not a subgroup for self-directed high-protein targeting.
caveat: High-protein evidence came from a small subset of older antenatal supplementation trials and does not address nonpregnant adults.

headline: Updated Cochrane review finds high-protein pregnancy supplementation increased SGA risk in one trial.
implication: Use this source to keep pregnancy high-protein supplementation out of adult protein-floor claims and to route pregnant users to clinician-supervised care.
caveat: Balanced energy/protein supplementation has separate pregnancy benefits and must not be collapsed into high-protein supplementation.

headline: WHO does not recommend high-protein supplementation in undernourished pregnancy.
implication: Protocol safety copy should treat pregnancy or attempts to conceive as a clinician-guidance boundary.
caveat: WHO guidance concerns pregnancy supplementation, especially undernourished populations, not nonpregnant adult food-based protein floors.

headline: High-protein low-carbohydrate/fiber diets worsened colonic-health metabolite profiles.
implication: Protein-floor guidance should preserve fiber/plant-food intake and not equate the protocol with very-low-carbohydrate dieting.
caveat: Small obese male controlled-feeding study; safety signal is tied to carbohydrate/fiber reduction and mechanistic metabolites.

headline: EASL supports adequate protein in cirrhosis under clinical supervision, not blanket restriction.
implication: Screen for liver disease and require clinician guidance; do not use liver guideline recommendations as healthy-adult efficacy claims.
caveat: Recommendations are disease-specific and depend on diagnosis, nutritional status, and clinical management.

headline: ESPEN frames liver-disease protein intake as individualized clinical nutrition.
implication: Use for liver-disease safety screening and clinician-supervision language rather than as a direct protocol-supporting trial.
caveat: Guideline evidence includes expert consensus and liver-disease-specific contexts; body-weight denominators may differ.

headline: Food-based 1.6 g/kg/day in older adults showed no adverse GI microbiota composition signal over 17 weeks.
implication: Supports a cautious digestive-safety statement when paired with limitations and metabolite gaps.
caveat: TMAO/proteolytic metabolites were not measured; fiber data were incomplete and the population was homogeneous.

headline: Target-range high protein was short-term tolerable in older women but shifted microbiota taxa.
implication: Supports GI symptom tracking and careful wording: feasibility does not equal microbiome neutrality.
caveat: Small older-women crossover; two-week periods and probiotic/prebiotic adjuncts limit attribution and generalizability.

headline: Large Nordic cohorts show mixed pregnancy context: no fetal-growth/mortality harm but modest preterm signal.
implication: Keep pregnancy outside protocol claims even though food-based cohort evidence is less alarming than older supplementation trials.
caveat: Observational food-intake evidence cannot establish causality and does not cover undernourished supplementation contexts.

headline: About 1.6 g/kg/day did not add strength benefit but showed no short-term renal/glycemic/cardiovascular biomarker harm.
implication: Use for null efficacy preservation and short-term safety context, not for promising superior resistance-training gains.
caveat: Moderate comparator already consumed about 1.0 g/kg/day; sample was small and previously untrained.

headline: High-protein calorie restriction altered microbiome composition without clear weight-loss superiority.
implication: Use as microbiome context and eligibility-screen reminder, not as direct protein-floor efficacy or safety proof.
caveat: Obesity, calorie restriction, percent-protein dosing, and exclusion criteria limit directness.

headline: Raising older adults to 1.2 g/kg adjusted body weight did not disturb microbiota or appetite.
implication: Useful as reassuring adjacent safety context, while keeping dose below target clearly labeled.
caveat: The achieved dose was below the 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protocol floor and used adjusted body weight.

headline: Direct 1.6 g/kg/day RCT shows body-fat and several cardiometabolic advantages versus 0.8 g/kg/day.
implication: A strong source-owned anchor for the protein-floor target in adults with obesity pursuing hypocaloric weight loss.
caveat: Protein and carbohydrate changed together, LDL favored the lower-protein comparator, and the sample was small.

headline: Longer 1.6 g/kg/day RCT supports body-composition and lipid benefits more than simple scale-weight superiority.
implication: Use as a primary direct-dose anchor for a protein floor, with claims framed around fat-mass partitioning, lipid patterns, and adherence rather than guaranteed extra pounds lost.
caveat: Comparator differed in carbohydrate; some stronger findings are completer or responder analyses.

headline: Prescribed 1.6 g/kg/day improved percent body-fat loss but did not clearly preserve total lean mass.
implication: Good direct-dose evidence for body-composition framing, especially fat-versus-lean partitioning, while avoiding overclaiming lean-mass preservation from diet alone.
caveat: Achieved protein was lower than the prescribed target and this overlaps with the Layman trial family.

headline: Controlled 1.6 g/kg/day dose improved fat-free-mass partitioning and muscle protein synthesis versus 0.8 g/kg/day.
implication: A key direct-dose anchor for setting the floor near 1.6 g/kg/day during energy deficit, especially when body composition is the endpoint.
caveat: Short controlled-feeding study with severe caloric restriction; free-living adherence and long-term safety are not established by this source.

headline: Large percent-protein RCT did not confirm superior long-term weight loss from higher protein assignment.
implication: Important boundary evidence: direct-dose claims should not be generalized into a blanket “higher protein always loses more weight” statement.
caveat: Not a clean 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protein-floor intervention; adherence drift reduced actual macronutrient separation.

headline: Higher-protein maintenance diet reduced regain and dropout after low-calorie weight loss.
implication: Supports a practical maintenance use case for the protein floor, especially after weight loss, while keeping direct-dose claims separate.
caveat: The exposure was protein-content assignment in a factorial GI trial, not a pure 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protein-floor target.

headline: Direct 1.5 g/kg/day trial did not preserve fat-free mass or resting energy expenditure in postmenopausal women.
implication: Important negative direct-dose boundary for claims about lean-mass and metabolic-rate preservation without exercise.
caveat: Possible handgrip-strength preservation signal; sample was postmenopausal women without exercise training.

headline: Higher-protein energy restriction matched weight loss overall, with triglyceride and fat-mass subgroup signals.
implication: Useful as cautious support for monitoring body composition and triglycerides during a protein-floor experiment, but not enough to promise superior scale weight loss.
caveat: Protein was delivered as a diet pattern rather than a clean 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day floor; women-only sample and short duration limit generalization.

headline: Higher-protein diet improved weight loss in metabolic syndrome, but broad biomarker separation was limited.
implication: Useful for a metabolic-risk protocol note: body-weight effects may occur without reliable improvements in every lab marker.
caveat: The high-protein target was about 1.34 g/kg/day, below the nominal 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day floor, and used protein shakes.

headline: Early higher-protein women-only RCT supports body-composition and triglyceride context, not direct floor claims.
implication: Useful background for why body composition and satiety are plausible endpoints, but not a direct protocol claim source.
caveat: Small, short, women-only, and not a clean 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day prescription.

headline: Higher-protein context trial improved selected metabolic signals but likely sat below the protein-floor dose.
implication: Useful for adjacent mechanism and safety context, not for direct protocol-dose claims.
caveat: Actual relative protein was later described around 1.0 g/kg/day in men and 1.2 g/kg/day in women, below the 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day target.

headline: Added protein reduced regain and increased satiety after weight loss.
implication: Supports protein as a maintenance-context lever for regain and satiety endpoints, but only as adjacent evidence for the protocol target.
caveat: Achieved protein was reported as a modest percent-energy increase, not as a 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day intervention.

headline: A 30 g/day protein supplement limited regain after weight loss.
implication: Supports a maintenance-context rationale for protein as a satiety and regain-control lever.
caveat: The intervention is an added-protein maintenance supplement, not direct evidence for the 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protein floor.

headline: Normal protein supported weight loss; elevated protein helped preserve REE and fat-free mass.
implication: Supports body-composition and expenditure endpoints for high-protein protocols, while preserving a boundary against overclaiming weight-loss necessity.
caveat: The elevated protein arm was around 1.2 g/kg/day, below the 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protocol floor.

headline: Protein supplements did not improve maintenance despite appetite and expenditure signals.
implication: A useful guardrail against overpromising weight-maintenance outcomes from supplements alone.
caveat: Post-weight-loss supplement trial, not a direct whole-diet 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protocol test.

headline: Higher protein supported lean-mass and satiety signals during weight loss.
implication: Relevant to protocol endpoints that include body composition and hunger, especially during dieting.
caveat: Weight-loss and female-only design limits directness to a general protein-floor protocol.

headline: During overfeeding, protein changed lean mass and expenditure but not fat storage.
implication: Helps bound claims: high protein can influence composition and expenditure, but it is not a substitute for energy-balance control.
caveat: Overfeeding context is not direct protein-floor evidence and should not be generalized to maintenance or weight-loss outcomes.

headline: Relatively higher protein, more than low carbohydrate, aligned with weight-loss and maintenance results.
implication: Supports including protein intake as a key exposure when interpreting weight and maintenance outcomes.
caveat: The high-protein dose was approximately 1.1 g/kg/day, below the 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day target, and energy restriction dominated the context.

headline: Extra protein above an already high refeed intake did not enhance FFM restoration.
implication: Supports a ceiling-effect boundary for protein supplementation once energy and protein are already sufficient.
caveat: Recovery after severe military energy deficit is not a normal protein-floor setting.

headline: High-protein total diet replacement increased expenditure and produced negative fat balance acutely.
implication: Supports mechanistic monitoring of energy expenditure and substrate oxidation, without proving long-term weight outcomes.
caveat: Formula-based 32-hour crossover in normal-weight adults is not direct protocol efficacy evidence.

headline: High-protein TDR altered appetite hormones but not subjective appetite sensations.
implication: Useful for mechanistic appetite interpretation and for avoiding overclaiming satiety from hormone changes alone.
caveat: Acute formula-based crossover; subjective appetite did not clearly improve.

headline: High protein did not preserve fat-free mass during severe high-altitude energy deficit.
implication: Important boundary: protein targets do not override inadequate energy availability and environmental stress.
caveat: Extreme high-altitude severe energy deficit makes this poorly generalizable to routine protein-floor use.

headline: Protein preloads raised CCK and reduced intake versus glucose in an acute male preload study.
implication: Supports appetite-hormone and short-term intake signals as plausible mechanisms to track.
caveat: Acute preload design is not direct evidence for a daily 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protein floor.

headline: Different protein preloads similarly reduced acute ad libitum intake versus glucose.
implication: Supports short-term appetite-mechanism plausibility for protein, with BMI-related hormone-response nuance.
caveat: Acute preload outcomes cannot establish long-term weight or satiety benefit from a daily protein floor.

headline: High-protein ketogenic feeding reduced hunger and intake versus high-protein medium-carbohydrate feeding.
implication: Useful for satiety and ad libitum intake context, with carbohydrate restriction treated as a cointervention.
caveat: Ketogenic status prevents assigning the effect to protein alone.

headline: High-protein diets reduced short-term energy intake, but did not prove low-protein overconsumption.
implication: Supports tracking spontaneous energy intake under high-protein conditions while preserving nuance around the protein-leverage model.
caveat: Twelve-day diet periods and percent-energy dosing limit directness to the protocol target.

headline: High beef-protein intake reduced short-term energy intake, but protein leverage was incomplete.
implication: Supports high-protein intake as a possible short-term energy-intake signal while preserving protein-source and duration boundaries.
caveat: Beef-source and 12-day crossover design are not direct protocol evidence.

headline: Higher-protein energy-restricted diets improved sleep-quality indexes in two trials.
implication: Adds sleep quality as a possible Murph signal during high-protein dieting experiments.
caveat: Sleep-index improvement is adjacent context and does not establish direct weight-maintenance or satiety efficacy.

headline: Protein intake did not affect appetite during high-altitude energy deficit.
implication: A useful negative boundary for satiety claims in extreme environmental and energy-deficit contexts.
caveat: High-altitude severe deficit is not a typical protein-floor setting.

headline: AHA 2001 cautions against overinterpreting early high-protein weight loss and poor diet-quality substitutions.
implication: Use for safety and claim-boundary language, especially around early scale changes and saturated-fat/fiber tradeoffs.
caveat: Historical statement; not direct evidence against a balanced protein floor with adequate fiber and monitoring.

headline: ISSN 2007 is historical support for the sports-nutrition 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day range.
implication: Use for background lineage, while preferring the 2017 update for current protocol-facing language.
caveat: Healthy exercising population and older position statement limit directness.

headline: Obesity guideline contextualizes weight outcomes but does not test protein-floor dosing.
implication: Use to avoid protein-only causal framing for weight change.
caveat: Not a protein-dose source.

headline: MSSE cross-publication supports athlete-context guidance but should not be double-counted.
implication: Keep as source-reconciliation and sports-guideline context.
caveat: Paywalled and overlapping with PMID 26920240.

headline: ISSN nutrient timing adds meal-distribution context to the daily protein floor.
implication: Use for implementation signals, not for direct efficacy claims about the total daily target.
caveat: Training-focused and timing-specific; daily dose remains the primary protocol variable.

headline: My New Gut position paper flags gut-health and fiber-displacement boundaries for high-protein weight-management diets.
implication: Use to require fiber and GI-tolerance tracking alongside protein grams.
caveat: Narrative/position-paper evidence should not be promoted as direct efficacy or harm proof.

headline: AHA 2021 keeps protein-floor implementation inside a cardiovascular dietary-pattern frame.
implication: Use for source-quality and diet-pattern guardrails rather than protein-dose efficacy.
caveat: Pattern guidance does not isolate protein amount effects.

headline: National Academies DRI provides the RDA comparator and AMDR context, not a protein-floor efficacy claim.
implication: Use to define baseline adequacy and avoid confusing RDA with a performance or weight-management target.
caveat: Reference-intake report is not an intervention trial of higher protein intake.

headline: Older-adult systematic review shows lean-mass and strength-with-exercise signals, plus important null and uncertain endpoints.
implication: Useful context for measuring lean mass, strength, and safety labs, but not a standalone protocol claim for all Murph users.
caveat: Older-adult RCTs varied in dose, baseline intake, cointerventions, and bias; no dose-response was identified.

headline: PROT-AGE supports higher protein targets in older adults, with kidney-disease boundaries.
implication: Helpful for population-tailoring and safety copy, not as direct proof that a 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day floor benefits all users.
caveat: Expert position paper; older adult illness categories should not be generalized to all protocol users.

headline: ESPEN links higher protein and exercise for older-adult muscle-function preservation.
implication: Useful to justify strength/function tracking and kidney boundary language for older users.
caveat: Consensus guidance for aging populations is not direct proof for all adults using a protein-floor experiment.

headline: Sports-nutrition position statement places active users near the protein-floor range.
implication: Use for active-user context and implementation nuance, not for universal efficacy claims.
caveat: Athlete populations and performance endpoints may not match general health self-experiments.

headline: ISSN 2017 gives the clearest sports-guideline overlap with the 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protocol band.
implication: Useful for active-user framing and meal-distribution suggestions while remaining adjacent rather than direct protocol proof.
caveat: Healthy exercising population; do not generalize to kidney disease, sedentary users, or medical nutrition therapy.

headline: AHRQ review finds protein-health evidence unclear for bone, kidney, and sarcopenia outcomes.
implication: Use to keep safety and chronic-disease uncertainty explicit, not to claim broad efficacy or broad harm.
caveat: The review excluded exercise-focused protein interventions, so it is not direct evidence for training-paired protein floors.

headline: Current U.S. Dietary Guidelines list 1.2-1.6 g/kg/day protein serving goals but are external guidance, not efficacy evidence.
implication: Use to contextualize a protein-forward target and food-quality guardrails while avoiding direct protocol claims.
caveat: The guideline overlaps the lower protein-floor band but does not evaluate 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day as a Murph protocol.

headline: High protein plus strength training showed no major oxidative-stress signal in older adults.
implication: Supports oxidative-stress and urea/BUN monitoring as safety endpoints in older protein-floor experiments.
caveat: Surrogate markers and supervised older-adult trial; urea/BUN rose, and women had more marker shifts.

headline: UK Biobank high-protein intake ≥1.8 g/kg/day was associated with higher CVD risk, especially after age 55.
implication: Use as observational cardiovascular safety context and a reason to stratify by age and baseline CVD risk.
caveat: Observational dietary questionnaire analysis; protein source, total diet, and residual confounding may explain part of the association.

headline: Older adults achieved about 1.6 g/kg/day with modest metabolomic shifts and no renal/liver disruption signal.
implication: Supports using renal/liver labs and metabolomic or cardiometabolic markers as safety monitors in a protein-floor experiment.
caveat: Supervised older-adult trial; not a hard adverse-event trial and not proof of long-term safety in people with kidney disease.

headline: Short-term 1.6-2.4 g/kg/day protein did not disrupt calcium homeostasis in healthy young adults.
implication: Useful for bone/calcium monitoring boundaries when a protein-floor experiment includes energy deficit.
caveat: Short duration and healthy young sample; not a fracture, osteoporosis, or long-term BMD trial.

headline: Higher protein during weight loss preserved modest lean mass but blunted insulin-action improvement in postmenopausal obesity.
implication: Treat as a population-specific metabolic caution and include glucose/insulin-sensitivity endpoints when applying a protein floor during weight loss.
caveat: Dose was 1.2 g/kg/day, below the protocol floor, and the sample was small and specific.

headline: Twice-RDA protein in older men increased TMAO and LDL, without differences in other CVD biomarkers or insulin sensitivity.
implication: Supports including lipid and TMAO/cardiometabolic biomarker monitoring for older users or high animal-protein patterns.
caveat: Small older-male trial; TMAO is a surrogate biomarker and not a clinical event.

headline: Controlled 1.6 g/kg/day protein in older men produced limited metabolomic changes.
implication: Supports using metabolomics or routine nitrogen-handling markers as measurement context rather than as efficacy promises.
caveat: Small male-only trial with exploratory metabolomics and short follow-up.

headline: High protein did not preserve testosterone or IGF-I during short-term energy deficit.
implication: Use to temper endocrine claims and to place FFM effects in a mechanism boundary rather than a hormone-preservation promise.
caveat: Short, small controlled-feeding study in energy deficit; not a long-term protocol safety trial.

headline: A 24-month calcium-replete higher-protein weight-loss diet did not worsen BMD in postmenopausal women.
implication: Useful for bone monitoring and for preserving null/safety findings in weight-loss contexts.
caveat: Not a clean g/kg protein-floor trial; postmenopausal low-BMD sample and calcium-replete design limit generalization.

headline: Extreme 4.4 g/kg/day protein did not improve body composition in young resistance-trained adults.
implication: Useful to avoid overselling protein beyond the floor; very high intake is not evidence of added benefit or comprehensive safety.
caveat: Dose is far above protocol target and safety labs/adverse events were not the primary focus.

headline: EAU stone guidance sets a lower animal-protein and purine boundary for stone-prone users.
implication: High-protein targets should be modified or clinically supervised for users with stone history, hyperuricosuria, uric-acid stones, or low urine pH.
caveat: Guideline boundary evidence is not a trial of the Murph protein-floor protocol in healthy users.

headline: NICE does not support claiming any specific diet as proven gout treatment.
implication: Protocol claims for gout-prone users should emphasize monitoring and clinical management, not dietary protein as a primary gout intervention.
caveat: NICE does not test a 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day protein floor and does not isolate protein source effects.

headline: AUA kidney-stone guidance requires protein-source limits in selected stone phenotypes.
implication: Protein-floor onboarding should screen for kidney-stone history and route stone formers toward urine chemistry monitoring and clinician-directed protein-source rules.
caveat: Guideline recommendations are not direct tests of Murph’s 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day target.

headline: ACR gout guidance makes serum-urate control and comorbidity status primary safety constraints.
implication: Protein-floor protocols should include gout/CKD/stone screening and avoid replacing treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy with dietary claims.
caveat: Guideline does not test high-protein intake; lifestyle recommendations are not direct protein-floor efficacy evidence.

headline: Recurrent hypercalciuric stone formers benefited from a normal-calcium, low-animal-protein, low-salt diet.
implication: A high-protein floor should be contraindicated or clinician-supervised in recurrent hypercalciuric calcium-stone formers.
caveat: Protein was bundled with salt and calcium strategy and tested only in men with a specific recurrent-stone phenotype.

headline: Added animal protein raised urinary calcium in a controlled metabolic setting.
implication: For stone-prone users, animal-protein-heavy versions of the protein floor should trigger urine-chemistry monitoring and clinician review.
caveat: Mechanistic short-term study in 11 healthy volunteers; not a hard-stone-outcome trial.

headline: Short-term healthy-adult renal markers were generally reassuring, but stone and long-term certainty were limited.
implication: Can support cautious renal-monitoring context for healthy users, while keeping stone-prone and CKD populations as exclusions or clinician-supervised cases.
caveat: Review did not prove long-term safety for all protein sources or for users with renal disease, stones, or gout.

headline: Observational evidence separates nondairy animal protein from dairy protein for stone risk.
implication: Protocol implementations should capture protein source and avoid a source-agnostic safety claim, especially in stone-prone users.
caveat: Prospective observational evidence cannot prove causality and credibility was low for most exposures.

headline: Umbrella review did not find proof that higher protein triggers stones or kidney disease, but long-term evidence is limited.
implication: Use to avoid alarmist kidney claims while still screening high-risk users and tracking renal/urinary endpoints.
caveat: Review-level evidence does not settle source-specific, very-long-term, CKD, gout, or recurrent-stone questions.

headline: Gout risk in men was source-specific: meat/seafood higher, dairy lower, total protein not the same signal.
implication: Protein-floor source tracking is essential for gout-prone users; total grams alone are not enough.
caveat: Prospective observational evidence cannot prove causality and does not test a protein-floor intervention.

headline: Two-year low-carb high-protein dieting did not show clear renal-marker harm, but urinary calcium rose.
implication: Supports cautious safety monitoring in lower-risk adults while preserving stone-risk guardrails.
caveat: Not a pure protein-floor dose trial and excluded serious illness; clinical stone events were not the primary endpoint.

headline: Incident gout risk differed by protein source in a large Singapore Chinese cohort.
implication: Protein-floor implementation should record protein source and flag purine/seafood/poultry-heavy patterns for gout-prone users.
caveat: Observational association, not a causal trial or direct protein-floor intervention.

headline: A DASH-style higher-protein feeding pattern modestly reduced serum urate.
implication: Useful for source-pattern nuance, but gout claims should remain conservative and monitoring-based.
caveat: Short controlled-feeding secondary analysis; not a gout flare trial or pure 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day intervention.

headline: Short wheat-gluten high-protein feeding lowered serum urate, but it is source-specific context.
implication: Useful for protein-source nuance: plant/gluten protein should not be grouped with meat/purine-heavy protein sources when discussing urate risk.
caveat: Small, short, hyperlipidemia sample; not a 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day free-living protein-floor trial.

headline: Animal-protein stone risk was observed only in leaner men in a long prospective cohort.
implication: Protein-floor safety review should stratify stone risk by baseline phenotype rather than apply a universal animal-protein rule.
caveat: Observational subgroup finding; not a randomized protein-dose trial.

headline: NHANES III links meat and seafood to higher serum urate and dairy to lower serum urate.
implication: Serum-urate monitoring should be interpreted with protein-source logs, not just total protein grams.
caveat: Cross-sectional and not causal; exact high-protein dose not tested.

headline: Low-animal-protein advice did not reduce calcium-stone recurrence in this trial.
implication: Do not overstate that lowering animal protein alone solves stone recurrence; still treat high-protein exposure cautiously in stone formers.
caveat: Null low-protein result does not establish high-protein safety; attrition and adherence limit inference.

headline: Dietary calcium was protective context, while animal protein had a modest observational stone signal.
implication: Stone-risk guardrails should include calcium and overall diet pattern, not just lower protein advice.
caveat: Observational cohort and older dietary assessment; not a randomized high-protein protocol.

headline: Six-month soy interventions did not increase serum urate in a narrow postmenopausal-women population.
implication: Soy can be considered separately from meat/seafood in urate-risk discussions, with population limits stated.
caveat: Not a gout flare study and not a mixed high-protein floor trial.

headline: EULAR gout guidance is management context, not protein-floor efficacy evidence.
implication: Use EULAR as a safety/context boundary for gout users rather than a source for protein-floor claims.
caveat: Guideline does not isolate protein dose or source effects for a Murph-style protocol.

headline: Low-animal-protein/high-fiber advice showed no advantage over fluids alone for recurrent calcium oxalate stones.
implication: Do not oversell protein reduction alone; also do not treat this null result as high-protein safety evidence.
caveat: Older small RCT and bundled advice; no direct high-protein exposure tested.

headline: A meal-kit CRHP protocol provides implementation design but no results yet.
implication: Useful for burden-reduction design ideas, not for claims about efficacy or safety.
caveat: Protocol-only; T2D/BMI>25 clinical population and percent-energy protein target.

headline: A small heart-failure feasibility study reported favorable short-term clinical and quality-of-life signals.
implication: Useful as a supervised-clinical implementation boundary, especially for screening and safety caveats.
caveat: Very small medically complex sample; not a direct protocol claim for general users.

headline: Fiber intake predicted weight loss and adherence in POUNDS Lost, providing diet-quality context for protein-floor design.
implication: Protein-floor experiments should monitor fiber displacement and diet quality as implementation outcomes.
caveat: This is not high-protein efficacy evidence.

headline: POUNDS Lost protein-intake markers were associated with greater weight-loss success.
implication: Supports measuring achieved protein intake, not just assignment, in protein-floor experiments.
caveat: Secondary associational analysis; participant count was not clearly available from accessible extraction records.

headline: A 1.6 g/kg/day higher-protein diet plus exercise context improved body-composition signals in adult women.
implication: Relevant for protein-floor experiments that also track exercise and lean mass.
caveat: Energy restriction, women-only sample, reduced carbohydrate, and exercise cointervention limit direct protocol use.

headline: Higher-protein diet improved short-term weight loss but long-term durability was uncertain.
implication: Useful for designing adherence and follow-up signals around a protein-floor experiment, but not for a direct 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day claim.
caveat: Protein target was percent energy, the trial was small, and late follow-up attrition was high.

headline: Pro-HEART improved cardiometabolic markers more with high protein, but weight loss was similar and clinical support was intensive.
implication: Useful for supervised implementation and monitoring endpoints, not for direct general-user claims.
caveat: Heart failure and diabetes create major population mismatch; short duration and high support burden limit translation.

headline: Higher percent-energy protein reduced appetite and ad libitum intake in a small controlled study.
implication: Supports measuring satiety and intake as implementation signals for a protein-floor experiment.
caveat: Sequential small study; not a direct g/kg/day free-living protocol test.

headline: PREVIEW found lower hunger with high-protein/low-GI maintenance but no clear weight-regain advantage.
implication: Useful for separating subjective satiety benefits from body-weight outcomes in protocol evaluation.
caveat: Not a direct g/kg target; long follow-up had attrition and incomplete compliance separation.

headline: Higher-protein DIOGENES diets reduced 12-month weight regain under a supported free-living model.
implication: Relevant for weight-maintenance and implementation planning, especially support burden and food-environment scaffolding.
caveat: Not a direct 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protocol and not a self-directed low-support intervention.

headline: DIOGENES participants rated higher-protein maintenance diets as more acceptable than low-protein diets.
implication: Supports including palatability and acceptability signals in a protein-floor experiment.
caveat: Subjective analysis in an obese post-weight-loss cohort; not a direct target-dose or efficacy test.

headline: Narrative renal-safety review separates healthy populations from susceptible groups.
implication: Use to justify renal-risk screening and CKD/diabetes caution, not to claim efficacy of the protein floor.
caveat: High-protein definitions and underlying study designs vary; narrative review only.

headline: Cohort evidence differs by baseline renal function.
implication: Use to require baseline kidney-risk screening and separate normal-kidney evidence from mild insufficiency.
caveat: Observational cohort; women-only and mostly white sample.

headline: Protein-kidney review supports healthy-vs-CKD separation.
implication: Useful for a renal safety boundary and lab-monitoring rationale, not for direct efficacy claims.
caveat: Narrative review and older literature base.

headline: Short-term 2.4 g/kg/day study shows renal hemodynamic response.
implication: Use to justify renal monitoring and avoid equating short-term marker shifts with long-term harm.
caveat: Very short and male-only; dose exceeds the 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protocol target.

headline: Broad meta-analysis shows mixed safety/tolerability signals rather than a clean renal claim.
implication: Use for adverse-event and surrogate-marker boundaries, especially GI tolerance and renal labs.
caveat: Not a clean g/kg target-dose comparison; kidney outcomes were surrogates.

headline: Controlled feeding protein-rich diet increased eGFR without resolving long-term kidney risk.
implication: Use to interpret eGFR changes as renal workload/adaptation signals requiring context.
caveat: Six-week diet periods and not a g/kg protein-floor prescription.

headline: Healthy-adult systematic review is useful context, not a target-dose renal trial.
implication: Use to frame evidence heterogeneity and endpoint selection for healthy adults.
caveat: Does not provide a single dose-specific estimate for 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day.

headline: High-protein diets changed renal workload markers in non-CKD adults.
implication: Use to require renal-function context and lab monitoring; do not treat higher GFR as either efficacy or harm by itself.
caveat: Surrogate markers and heterogeneous trials; long-term CKD outcomes not established.

headline: Adverse-effect review identifies safety domains for above-RDA protein intake.
implication: Use to preserve adverse-event and symptom monitoring categories.
caveat: Does not isolate the Murph target or provide a causal estimate for healthy adults.

headline: Long-term renal review emphasizes uncertainty and protein-source boundaries.
implication: Use to avoid overclaiming long-term kidney safety from short-term trials.
caveat: Narrative review and mixed evidence base.

headline: Healthy-adult meta-analysis does not show adverse GFR change from higher protein.
implication: Use to contextualize renal lab changes in healthy adults without claiming long-term CKD safety.
caveat: Surrogate kidney-function outcome and bias concerns; not a CKD-incidence trial.

headline: Cohort links high-protein plus hyperfiltration to rapid renal decline.
implication: Use as a cautionary monitoring signal and a reason not to dismiss hyperfiltration.
caveat: Observational association; residual confounding and diet measurement error remain possible.

headline: Nephrology review preserves a conservative renal-risk mechanism.
implication: Use to justify CKD screening, renal monitoring, and protein-source caution.
caveat: Mechanistic/narrative evidence should not be promoted to causal proof for healthy users.

headline: KDOQI guideline makes CKD a medical-nutrition boundary.
implication: Use to exclude or clinician-supervise CKD users before applying a protein-floor target.
caveat: Guideline applies to CKD care, not healthy adults.

headline: ESPEN guideline defines hospitalized kidney disease as clinician-supervised.
implication: Use to route AKD/CKD and hospitalized users away from generic protein-floor claims.
caveat: Not relevant to healthy ambulatory efficacy; kidney-disease context only.

headline: 1.6 g/kg/day trial measured kidney markers and found creatinine changes.
implication: Use for lower-bound target-dose safety monitoring, not as a long-term kidney-safety guarantee.
caveat: Eight weeks, older men only, and surrogate renal markers.

headline: Training trial overlaps 1.6 g/kg/day and includes 3.2 g/kg/day high-dose boundary.
implication: Use to support lab monitoring and caution against assuming more protein is better.
caveat: Trained young men only and no long-term renal outcomes.

headline: KDIGO guideline anchors CKD screening and management boundaries.
implication: Use to require renal risk triage before applying high-protein protocol claims.
caveat: CKD guideline, not healthy protein-floor evidence.

headline: Nursing-home ONS trial found no renal deterioration over eight weeks.
implication: Use for supervised supplement safety context, especially older/frail populations.
caveat: Not a free-living 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protein-floor protocol.

headline: Very-low-carbohydrate weight-loss trial is adjacent renal-safety context.
implication: Use only when considering protein increases embedded inside weight-loss/low-carbohydrate patterns.
caveat: Protein-specific causal effect cannot be isolated.

headline: T2D high-protein weight-loss trial found no overall renal-function change.
implication: Use for disease-context safety boundaries, not healthy protocol claims.
caveat: Diabetes and weight-loss context; not a free-living protein-floor trial.

headline: Older-adult cohort found no major kidney-decline impact from higher protein.
implication: Use as observational context alongside conflicting cohort and CKD-boundary evidence.
caveat: Observational design and FFQ measurement limit causal inference.

headline: One-year T2D low-carb high-protein trial found no adverse renal-marker effect.
implication: Use as supervised clinical adjacent evidence, not a healthy protein-floor proof.
caveat: Cannot isolate protein from carbohydrate restriction and weight loss.

headline: Small trained-male crossover found no deleterious markers at >3 g/kg/day.
implication: Use as high-dose adjacent safety context only.
caveat: Small, short, trained-male sample; not powered for kidney disease outcomes.

headline: Low-carbohydrate renal meta-analysis is adjacent, not direct protein-floor evidence.
implication: Use for renal-monitoring context when protein increases inside low-carbohydrate patterns.
caveat: Protein dose and carbohydrate restriction are confounded.

headline: Small trained-male crossover found no renal/liver/lipid harm at very high protein.
implication: Use as adjacent high-dose safety context, not a universal safety guarantee.
caveat: Small, highly selected resistance-trained male sample and self-reported intake.

headline: Plant-versus-animal protein review informs source quality, not renal claims.
implication: Use to keep source quality separate from dose-floor efficacy and kidney safety claims.
caveat: Renal endpoints are not the main evidence target.

headline: T2D source-comparison trial is adjacent source-quality evidence.
implication: Use for source-quality and diabetes context, not direct renal or healthy protocol claims.
caveat: Short T2D trial and not kidney-outcome powered.

headline: Tehran cohort suggests plant-protein source context for CKD risk.
implication: Use for source-quality context and not as causal protocol evidence.
caveat: Observational FFQ data and residual confounding.

headline: T2D high- versus normal-protein trial is adjacent clinical context.
implication: Use for diabetes/source-quality boundaries, not healthy renal-safety claims.
caveat: Diabetes population and non-renal primary focus.

headline: Protein-supplement review supports supplement-specific renal caution.
implication: Use to separate supplement-heavy implementation from whole-food protein-floor evidence.
caveat: Narrative review and not dose-specific to Murph.

headline: Prospective-cohort meta-analysis reports lower CKD risk associations, not causal protection.
implication: Use as observational context that complicates simple high-protein harms narratives.
caveat: Residual confounding and protein-source differences limit protocol claims.

headline: Older athlete study found no measured renal impairment below ~2.8 g/kg/day.
implication: Use as low-priority athlete-specific safety context only.
caveat: Older, athlete-only, and not a long-term randomized kidney-outcome study.

headline: Older-adult protein-advice trial is implementation context, not renal evidence.
implication: Use only for feasibility/context signals about dietary advice to raise protein.
caveat: Dose below Murph target and kidney endpoints not central.

headline: A moderate repeated post-exercise protein pattern increased acute myofibrillar protein synthesis.
implication: Supports optional experiment signals around per-meal dose and workout-adjacent spacing.
caveat: Acute whey tracer study in young trained men; not evidence that total daily protein-floor users need this schedule.

headline: Even meal distribution improved 24-hour muscle protein synthesis in a small controlled-feeding crossover.
implication: A plausible optional distribution signal for users tracking per-meal protein.
caveat: Very small short-term physiology study; MPS is not the same as long-term lean-mass gain.

headline: Protein quantity improved net balance, but meal pattern did not show a clear independent effect.
implication: Supports treating the daily protein floor as primary and distribution as optional/uncertain.
caveat: Short metabolic study in healthy older adults; not long-term clinical efficacy evidence.

headline: Even protein distribution did not improve lean mass, strength, function, or anabolic response over 8 weeks.
implication: Distribution should remain optional and not be promoted as a required protocol mechanism.
caveat: Small older-adult trial and total protein below the 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day floor.

headline: Even distribution did not alter body-composition responses during weight loss plus resistance training.
implication: Avoid promoting meal distribution as a proven body-composition lever for the base protein-floor protocol.
caveat: Energy restriction and resistance training context; protein intake not framed as a 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day floor.

headline: Even distribution did not improve MPS or amino-acid utilization versus skewed distribution.
implication: Supports conservative language around meal distribution and keeps the daily floor separate from timing rules.
caveat: Short-term older-adult physiology study, not a long-term outcome trial.

headline: At 1.5 g/kg/day in two meals, net balance improved but MPS was not significantly different.
implication: Supports the daily target as a protein-balance signal while keeping timing and measurement tolerability caveats visible.
caveat: Acute two-meal physiology study; D2O nausea affected completion and does not equal a protein-intake adverse event.

headline: PROMISS secondary analysis did not find distribution metrics useful for strength or walking outcomes.
implication: Useful as a guardrail against adding complex distribution targets to the base protocol.
caveat: Exploratory secondary analysis; associations are not causal and participants had low habitual protein intake.

headline: Pulse feeding improved nitrogen-balance physiology in a small elderly-women study.
implication: Supports keeping meal distribution as a plausible adjacent variant, especially for aging physiology.
caveat: Small, short, older-women-only study; not direct evidence for a free-living 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protein floor.

headline: Even distribution with a higher-protein breakfast improved hypertrophy signals in young men during resistance training.
implication: Supports optional distribution experiments for trained users, especially breakfast protein tracking.
caveat: Young men only; daily protein below protocol floor and resistance training is a co-intervention.

headline: Even distribution improved some whole-body balance signals but not muscle FSR.
implication: Good source for nuanced protocol-adjacent timing language and biomarker selection.
caveat: Short controlled physiology study in healthy older adults; not a clinical-outcome trial.

headline: Even distribution did not influence body-composition changes during weight loss in women.
implication: Supports keeping meal-distribution claims separate from daily protein-floor claims.
caveat: Women-only weight-loss sample; not a free-living protein-floor target trial.

headline: At 2 g/kg/day, exact workout-adjacent timing did not show a between-group advantage in trained men.
implication: Supports not overprescribing timing precision for the base protein floor while monitoring labs when available.
caveat: Young trained men only, no lower-protein comparator, 8 weeks, and 9 withdrawals.

headline: Higher protein helped appetite signals, but higher meal frequency did not clearly add benefit.
implication: Useful for protocol-adjacent adherence design: target protein may matter more than making users eat many times per day.
caveat: Energy-restricted overweight/obese men only; meal frequency and protein dose are bundled differently from the base protein-floor protocol.

headline: Protein-pacing improved performance/body-composition signals whether delivered by foods or supplements.
implication: Useful for optional implementation variants when users need meal structure or supplement support.
caveat: Small completed sample and bundled protein-pacing program; not direct isolated daily protein-floor evidence.

headline: Review-level distribution evidence is mixed and heterogeneous.
implication: Use this source to temper claims and guide grouping, not as a standalone efficacy proof.
caveat: Narrative review; source-owned findings should remain distinct from primary trial findings.

headline: High-protein breakfast improved satiety but not body composition or cardiometabolic markers.
implication: Supports separating appetite signals from body-composition claims.
caveat: Breakfast-only young-women trial; not total daily protein-floor evidence.

headline: Pulse feeding did not improve protein retention in young women.
implication: Highlights population-specificity and prevents extrapolating older-adult pulse-feeding results to everyone.
caveat: Small short physiology study; not a daily protein-floor trial.

headline: Pulse feeding improved lean-mass measures in malnourished elderly patients, with limited functional signal.
implication: Relevant only for supervised clinical-adjacent boundaries, not healthy-user protocol claims.
caveat: Hospitalized malnourished elderly population; clinical feeding context and functional endpoints limit generalization.

headline: Post-exercise distribution changed turnover/synthesis signals without clear net-balance separation.
implication: Supports collecting timing/workout context without turning it into a direct protocol requirement.
caveat: Acute whey study in trained men; no long-term body-composition endpoint.

headline: 20 g and 40 g whey stimulated MPS, but 40 g increased oxidation/urea without clear added MPS.
implication: Useful for optional per-meal-dose tracking and nitrogen-waste context.
caveat: Acute whey study in trained young men; not a daily protein-floor outcome trial.

headline: Breakfast/lunch protein supplementation increased lean tissue mass in older adults.
implication: Supports optional older-adult supplementation/timing variants.
caveat: Timing and total protein dose changed together; supplement-based trial, not base diet-only protein floor.

headline: High-protein breakfast reduced postprandial ghrelin in an acute crossover study.
implication: Useful for appetite-mechanism context and breakfast-protein variant design.
caveat: Acute healthy-men study; no daily floor or long-term outcome test.

headline: Timed whey plus exercise reduced visceral fat and improved insulin-resistance signals.
implication: Relevant for bundled protein-pacing/exercise variants, not the base daily target.
caveat: Protein timing, whey supplementation, and exercise training are not isolated.

headline: Balanced protein plus resistance training restored MPS during energy restriction in older men.
implication: Useful for optional training and weight-loss context, not for base target claims.
caveat: Bundled energy restriction, resistance training, and balanced distribution; older men only.

headline: Protein-enriched foods increased daily protein intake in older rehab patients.
implication: Useful for source-delivery and adherence variants.
caveat: Rehabilitation-centre implementation trial; not an efficacy trial for the base protein floor.

headline: Breakfast protein/fiber did not clearly change appetite or lunch intake in a small crossover.
implication: Tempering source for breakfast-protein satiety claims.
caveat: Acute small lab study; not a daily high-protein target trial.

headline: Protein pacing plus multicomponent exercise improved performance in trained women.
implication: Relevant to optional active-user pacing variants.
caveat: Protein pacing is bundled with exercise training and trained-women sample.

headline: Protein-pacing caloric restriction was linked with body-composition and maintenance benefits.
implication: Relevant for weight-loss variants, not base protein-floor claims.
caveat: Sample count and detailed contrasts not extracted here; caloric restriction and protein pacing are bundled.

headline: 40 g whey exceeded 20 g for acute MPS after whole-body resistance exercise.
implication: Useful per-meal-dose boundary for trained users and high training-volume contexts.
caveat: Acute whey study; sample count not extracted here and no long-term outcome endpoint.

headline: Breakfast protein supplementation was reported to benefit skeletal muscle mass in older adults.
implication: Potential optional morning-protein variant source.
caveat: Participant count and intervention details were not fully extracted in this batch draft; do not use for direct base-protocol claims.

headline: IF plus protein pacing outperformed caloric restriction for weight and visceral fat in extracted summary.
implication: Relevant to bundled weight-loss variants, not daily protein-floor claims.
caveat: Intermittent fasting and protein pacing are bundled; participant count/duration not extracted here.

headline: Large post-exercise protein bolus produced a prolonged anabolic response in acute physiology.
implication: Useful for challenging rigid per-meal ceilings while preserving caution.
caveat: Acute lab bolus study; sample count not extracted here and no long-term clinical outcome.

headline: Protein-rich dairy breakfast improved satiety/concentration but not clearly daily energy intake.
implication: Good optional breakfast endpoint source; not efficacy evidence for the daily protein floor.
caveat: Acute crossover in young females with overweight/obesity.

headline: Protein-pacing plus intermittent fasting shifted microbiome/metabolomic profiles in a bundled trial.
implication: Mechanistic context only; avoid using microbiome signals as direct protocol efficacy evidence.
caveat: IF and protein pacing are bundled; sample count/duration not extracted and causality for protein alone is not established.

headline: A 1.6 g/kg/day higher-protein weight-loss diet improved glucose/insulin dynamics without greater weight loss.
implication: Supports including fasting glucose and postprandial insulin/glucose as metabolic readouts for Protein Floor experiments.
caveat: Small women-only trial; carbohydrate reduction and energy restriction prevent a protein-only interpretation.

headline: Long-term high-protein/lower-carbohydrate assignment did not outperform standard protein for weight or lab changes.
implication: Counters simple claims that higher protein reliably improves cardiometabolic labs beyond energy restriction.
caveat: Adherence deteriorated and the comparison also changed carbohydrate intake.

headline: Large maintenance trial did not identify high protein as the clear cardiometabolic benefit driver.
implication: Supports separating weight-loss and glycemic-index effects from protein effects.
caveat: Multi-arm maintenance design after run-in weight loss; not a direct protein-floor target.

headline: Long-term RCT meta-analysis found only a small fasting-insulin advantage and little else.
implication: Supports conservative metabolic-lab claims for Protein Floor.
caveat: Trials were low-fat weight-loss diets with variable adherence and bias risk.

headline: Controlled feeding found no broad high-protein advantage for insulin sensitivity or lipids.
implication: Supports conservative metabolic-lab claims for the protocol.
caveat: Short duration and low-carbohydrate factorial design limit directness.

headline: Large RCT meta-analysis found small favorable effects on selected cardiometabolic markers.
implication: Supports a modest-effect framing for Protein Floor metabolic signals.
caveat: Heterogeneity and percent-energy dosing limit direct conversion to 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day.

headline: High-protein/lower-carbohydrate advice produced mixed long-term cardiometabolic signals in obese adults with T2D.
implication: Supports blood pressure and renal-related monitoring but does not establish broad superiority.
caveat: Attrition, weight regain, and carbohydrate differences limit direct application.

headline: A small T2D trial found blood-pressure benefit but no clear glycemic advantage for high protein.
implication: Supports a cautious, endpoint-specific interpretation rather than global metabolic claims.
caveat: Very small trial; diet arms changed carbohydrate and protein together.

headline: High protein modestly outperformed a higher-fiber diet for weight, fat, and diastolic blood pressure over 8 weeks.
implication: Supports including body composition and blood pressure as experiment signals.
caveat: Short energy-restricted trial; high-protein arm also had less carbohydrate/fiber.

headline: T2D meta-analysis favored high protein for short-term weight and HbA1c but not lipids or fasting glucose.
implication: Supports HbA1c as a candidate endpoint in metabolically at-risk subgroups.
caveat: Short trials in T2D; carbohydrate displacement and influential studies limit directness.

headline: Carbohydrate-reduced high-protein feeding improved glycemic and hepatic-fat markers in T2D.
implication: Supports glycemic endpoint monitoring in metabolically at-risk users.
caveat: Protein, carbohydrate, and fat changed together; small T2D study.

headline: Large 3-year prevention trial found no high-protein/low-GI advantage for T2D incidence.
implication: Supports conservative long-term prevention claims.
caveat: High-protein was bundled with low GI and physical-activity arms; adherence was difficult.

headline: Carbohydrate-to-protein substitution lowered lipids in a controlled setting, but dose details are incomplete.
implication: Supports tracking total cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C, and triglycerides when people shift calories from carbohydrate to protein.
caveat: Not a direct 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day protocol test, and sample-size/duration details were not extracted.

headline: High-protein diet plus exercise improved weight and some lipids, but attribution is confounded.
implication: Supports tracking exercise as a co-variable in protein-floor experiments.
caveat: No direct 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day dose; diet and exercise effects were intertwined.

headline: Assigned high protein did not outperform high carbohydrate, but reported protein intake correlated with weight loss.
implication: Supports tracking achieved protein as a continuous exposure.
caveat: Correlation by reported intake should not be treated as randomized causal evidence.

headline: T2D 12-month trial found no superior metabolic benefit for high-protein advice.
implication: Supports conservative long-term glycemic and cardiometabolic claims.
caveat: T2D clinical diet-advice setting; protein and carbohydrate changed together.

headline: Near-target high protein preserved lean mass but did not improve cardiometabolic markers beyond normal protein.
implication: Supports lean-mass endpoints more strongly than metabolic lab claims.
caveat: Dose was about 1.4 g/kg/day and trial was short and male-only.

headline: High-protein low-fat diet did not outperform higher-carbohydrate low-fat diet in T2D.
implication: Supports cautious interpretation of metabolic lab improvements during weight loss.
caveat: Exercise advice and weight loss were shared co-interventions.

headline: High-protein diet improved several cardiometabolic and inflammatory markers in women with obesity.
implication: Supports considering HOMA-IR, LDL-C, blood pressure, and inflammation markers in subgroup experiments.
caveat: Short, women-only obesity trial; protein target was 25% energy, not explicit g/kg/day.

headline: Short inpatient high-protein feeding improved insulin resistance and glycemic variability.
implication: Supports insulin and CGM variability as candidate experiment signals.
caveat: Short, small, open-label, no-washout inpatient trial in insulin-resistant women.

headline: Recent network meta-analysis favored higher-protein diet nodes for body-composition outcomes.
implication: Supports body-composition tracking but not direct metabolic causality from protein alone.
caveat: Network indirectness and macronutrient displacement are central limitations.

headline: Small T2D crossover study reported improved glucose control with 30% protein/40% carbohydrate.
implication: Supports glycemic endpoints in T2D-like contexts, with strong caveats.
caveat: Small, short, untreated T2D study; protein increase and carbohydrate decrease were coupled.

headline: Moderate higher-protein diets did not differentially improve most cardiometabolic markers.
implication: Supports conservative lab expectations and source-specific caveats.
caveat: Short trial, exploratory biomarkers, postmenopausal women, and protein-source confounding.

headline: Glutamate-rich high-protein feeding produced adverse lipid-mechanism signals in a small mechanistic study.
implication: Supports triglyceride/VLDL monitoring and protein-source caveats.
caveat: Very small mechanistic male study; not representative of all protein-floor diets.

headline: LoBAG diet improved glucose in a very small untreated T2D crossover trial.
implication: Supports glucose monitoring when higher protein also reduces carbohydrate.
caveat: Very small, all-male, short, low-carbohydrate T2D study; long-term effects unknown.

headline: Protein overfeeding study is mechanistic context, not protocol efficacy evidence.
implication: Supports recording energy balance when interpreting protein-related metabolic labs.
caveat: Participants were overfed by about 40%, and high-protein intake exceeded the target range.

headline: Named-diet trial cannot isolate protein from low-carbohydrate diet pattern.
implication: Useful for context on diet-pattern confounding, not protocol efficacy.
caveat: Atkins effects cannot be attributed to a 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day protein target.

headline: Post-sleeve 2.0 g/kg ideal-body-weight protein favored fat-mass, FFM, and RMR outcomes in a male bariatric population.
implication: Useful as clinical context for body-composition, resting-energy-expenditure, adherence, and renal-function monitoring, but not as direct proof for a free-living general-adult Protein Floor protocol.
caveat: Male-only post-laparoscopic-sleeve-gastrectomy population; protein prescribed by ideal body weight; clinical postoperative context; accessible abstract lacks absolute effect sizes, randomization detail, and adverse-event detail beyond renal-function reporting.

headline: Older consumers varied in acceptance of protein-enriched food carriers.
implication: Useful for product choice and adherence planning.
caveat: No health outcome or achieved intake was tested.

headline: Higher-protein macronutrient substitution improved glycemic response in type 2 diabetes.
implication: Relevant to glucose-monitoring endpoints and metabolic-boundary interpretation.
caveat: Clinical diabetes evidence should not be generalized to healthy users or used as protein-floor efficacy proof.

headline: High-protein diet mechanisms are plausible, but early weight-loss evidence was inconsistent and short term.
implication: Use only as background, not as direct efficacy evidence.
caveat: Narrative reviews are lower certainty and should not override trial-level null findings.

headline: Higher habitual protein intake was associated with less lean-mass loss in older adults.
implication: Supports baseline-intake stratification and observational context.
caveat: Do not infer causality or direct protocol efficacy.

headline: Higher protein during energy restriction supported muscle retention/physical function in older women.
implication: Useful older-female weight-loss context for lean-mass endpoints.
caveat: Energy restriction and exact dose boundary limit direct protocol use.

headline: IAAO estimated protein requirement in octogenarian women above classic EAR values but below the Murph floor.
implication: Useful requirement-method context for older-old women.
caveat: Requirement estimation is not evidence that 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day improves outcomes.

headline: Protein-enriched regular foods increased intake in hospitalized older adults.
implication: Useful for implementation/delivery mechanics, not direct efficacy.
caveat: Three-day hospital exposure and a lower target than the protocol floor.

headline: IAAO estimated older women’s protein requirement above conventional RDA assumptions.
implication: Supports requirement-method context around age strata.
caveat: Does not demonstrate clinical benefit from 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day.

headline: IAAO estimated older men’s protein requirement/RDA above current EAR assumptions.
implication: Useful for requirement-method context and older male strata.
caveat: Not outcome evidence for 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day.

headline: Protein-enriched familiar foods may help institutionalized older adults increase intake.
implication: Useful for adherence/product-delivery strategies.
caveat: No controlled efficacy inference and target is below 1.5 g/kg/day.

headline: Protein-enriched familiar foods improved protein intake in hospitalized older patients.
implication: Useful for delivery/adherence evidence and clinical population boundaries.
caveat: Hospital intake improvement should not be generalized to healthy home users.

headline: Whole-egg high-protein diet supported lean retention but not broader cardiometabolic or inflammation improvements.
implication: Useful for source-quality/source-specific outcome boundaries.
caveat: Do not generalize whole-egg diet results to all protein sources.

headline: IAAO postexercise estimates in trained females fall within/near the Murph target range.
implication: Mechanistic support for active-user strata and postexercise anabolism endpoints.
caveat: Acute whole-body anabolism is not a clinical outcome and used amino acid feeding.

headline: Postexercise whole-body anabolism in trained men plateaued near 2.0 g/kg/day.
implication: Mechanistic context for active users and the upper bound of the Murph target.
caveat: Acute, small, trained-male study; urinary nitrogen markers require safety-context separation.

headline: IAAO estimated Chinese older-adult protein requirements modestly above current estimates.
implication: Adds ethnicity/age-strata requirement-method context.
caveat: Not an outcome trial and not a direct 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day test.

headline: Protocol proposes high-protein diet with/without power training in pre-frail/frail adults.
implication: Useful for protocol-design context and frailty-boundary planning.
caveat: No efficacy or safety results should be extracted from a protocol paper.

headline: Protein above RDA lowered visceral fat but did not improve cardiometabolic risk markers.
implication: Useful for VAT/cardiometabolic endpoint boundaries in older men.
caveat: 1.3 g/kg/day is below the Murph target and trial population was functionally limited.

headline: PROMISS protocol defines personalized advice to reach ≥1.2 g/kg adjusted body weight/day.
implication: Useful for baseline-intake and advice-delivery design.
caveat: Protocol paper has no efficacy results and target is below 1.5 g/kg/day.

headline: Low protein-awareness may limit uptake of higher-protein advice in older adults.
implication: Useful for education/adherence features in Murph protocol design.
caveat: No health outcome was tested.

headline: Additional protein at a 1.5 g/kg normalized-body-weight target did not preserve body composition during formula-based obesity treatment.
implication: Important null/negative adjacent evidence near the Murph lower bound.
caveat: Severe energy restriction and morbid obesity treatment are not typical Murph conditions.

headline: Adding 20 g/day protein did not improve older-adult muscle-function outcomes over 12 weeks.
implication: Important null boundary for modest supplementation in older adults.
caveat: Incremental protein dose may not reach Murph target; details require full paper extraction.

headline: IAAO in sarcopenic older adults estimated an RNI around 1.54 g/kg/day.
implication: Directly relevant to requirement-method context near the Murph lower bound for sarcopenia.
caveat: Requirement estimates do not prove health-outcome benefits and population is sarcopenic.

headline: Higher-protein ad libitum low-fat diet improved weight and fat loss in adults with obesity.
implication: Useful as adjacent evidence that protein emphasis can alter energy-balance outcomes, but not as a direct g/kg protein-floor claim.
caveat: Percent-energy protein, obesity treatment, and controlled food access limit directness to a 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day self-experiment.

headline: Higher protein reduced lean-mass loss during weight loss in postmenopausal women.
implication: Supports older-female/body-composition context at the lower edge of the protocol target.
caveat: Small, hypocaloric, postmenopausal obesity trial; dose precision remains an extraction boundary.

headline: Protein-for-carbohydrate substitution changed lipid markers in a short-term hypercholesterolemia setting.
implication: Relevant for cardiometabolic monitoring, not for efficacy claims about the protein-floor target.
caveat: Dose was percent-energy based and the population had elevated cholesterol.

headline: Higher protein affected regional body composition but not total composition in overweight/obese adults.
implication: Useful for sex-strata and body-composition endpoint selection.
caveat: Regional effects and sex-specific analyses should not be generalized into a universal protein-floor benefit.

headline: A 1.7 g/kg/day high-protein diet did not preserve lean mass during older-adult energy restriction.
implication: Important null boundary for the protein-floor target in an older weight-loss stratum.
caveat: Null result was in an energy-deficit intervention, not a resistance-training or maintenance context.

headline: Higher-protein weight-loss diets in older adults favored lean-mass retention and fat loss in synthesis.
implication: Provides strata-level context for older adults and energy-restriction endpoints.
caveat: Dose thresholds and weight-loss contexts are not equivalent to a universal 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day floor.

headline: Adherence depends on habit fit, knowledge, taste, convenience, and packaging.
implication: Useful for Murph burden/adherence design when asking users to sustain a protein floor.
caveat: Qualitative implementation data should not be treated as efficacy evidence.

headline: Higher protein improved appendicular lean-mass/function signals in elderly men.
implication: Useful population-stratum support for older male lean-mass endpoints.
caveat: Dose and cointervention details need full-text extraction before use as a direct protocol claim.

headline: Protein above the RDA did not improve lean mass or function in functionally limited older men.
implication: Important null evidence for older low-intake men and functional endpoints.
caveat: Tested 1.3 g/kg/day, below the 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day target.

headline: Higher-protein adherence was linked with more favorable body-composition changes in older women exercising.
implication: Supports exercise-context endpoint design but not a diet-only claim.
caveat: Adherence and cointervention effects should be separated before protocol synthesis.

headline: Higher-protein energy-restricted meal plan reduced body mass/fat mass in older adults with obesity.
implication: Relevant to weight-loss variant boundaries near 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day.
caveat: Control condition and energy restriction prevent direct attribution to the protein floor alone.

headline: Two advice strategies raised older adults’ protein intake over four weeks.
implication: Useful for feasibility/adherence mechanics for a protein-floor protocol.
caveat: Does not test clinical efficacy or the full 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day target.

headline: Euenergetic high-protein diet did not cause significant weight loss in women with normal-weight obesity.
implication: Helps prevent overpromising weight loss when calories are held constant.
caveat: Body-composition findings and achieved g/kg dose should be rechecked before any dose-specific claim.

headline: Personalized advice to reach ≥1.2 g/kg aBW/day improved physical-function signals and cost-effectiveness in older low-intake adults.
implication: Useful implementation context for older adults whose baseline intake is low.
caveat: Dose is below protocol target and the endpoint is clinical function, not general wellness.

headline: Health Council review found insufficiently convincing benefit for raising protein above 0.8 g/kg/day in already-adequate older adults.
implication: Important caution against universal older-adult benefit claims.
caveat: Does not rule out benefit in low-intake, exercising, ill, or sarcopenic subgroups.

headline: Higher protein at 1.2 g/kg did not improve satiety or weight loss over normal protein in an 8-week low-energy diet.
implication: Null satiety boundary for weight-loss contexts below the target range.
caveat: Dose below 1.5 g/kg/day and all groups were on low-energy partial diet replacement.

headline: PROMISS secondary analysis supports feasibility of personalized protein-increase advice in older low-intake adults.
implication: Useful for adherence, burden, and baseline-intake stratification.
caveat: Do not convert feasibility and 1.2 g/kg-aBW target evidence into a direct 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day claim.

headline: Protein-rich meals and snacks can raise older adults’ protein intake cost-effectively.
implication: Useful for practical delivery and cost-burden considerations.
caveat: Implementation economics should not be used as efficacy evidence.

headline: Older-adult perceptions support food-first implementation planning, not efficacy claims.
implication: Use as implementation context only, especially for older adults who may prefer whole-food strategies over supplements.
caveat: Directness: Implementation context; no intervention outcome evidence. Limitations: Pilot design; participant count not verified in this extraction; self-reported perceptions; no health outcomes. Population mismatch: Older adults’ perceptions may differ from younger users or athletes.

headline: Protein-increase advice can change sustainability metrics through source mix.
implication: Use as sustainability/source-quality context; protein-increase advice should track food-source mix as well as grams.
caveat: Directness: Implementation/sustainability context; not efficacy evidence. Limitations: Secondary analysis; participant count not verified here; older low-protein sample; environmental-impact modeling depends on assumptions. Population mismatch: Older European adults may not represent global Murph users or athletes.

headline: Food-first review supports source/matrix awareness but is not trial evidence.
implication: Use as mechanism/context only; do not treat as a trial outcome source.
caveat: Directness: Mechanistic/context review; no direct protocol test. Limitations: Narrative review; not a quantitative meta-analysis; no single population or protocol dose. Population mismatch: Athlete/exercise literature may not apply to all Murph users.

headline: EPIC-CVD preserves a null overall source association with selected observational substitution signals.
implication: Use as observational context only; preserve the null overall CVD association and avoid causal claims.
caveat: Directness: Observational context; not direct protocol evidence. Limitations: Dietary measurement error; residual confounding; case-cohort design; subgroup and substitution results are hypothesis-generating. Population mismatch: European cohort participants may differ from current Murph users and free-living experimenters.

headline: Large cohorts provide source-pattern mortality context, not causal protein-floor evidence.
implication: Use as observational source-quality context only; do not claim causality or direct protocol efficacy.
caveat: Directness: Observational context; not intervention evidence. Limitations: Self-reported diet; residual confounding; substitution modeling; not a protein-dose intervention; healthcare professional cohorts. Population mismatch: US health professionals may not represent general Murph users.

headline: Higher plant-to-animal protein ratios are observationally linked to lower CVD/CAD risk but not direct protocol efficacy.
implication: Use as observational source-mix context only; do not claim that changing plant-to-animal ratio causally improves outcomes for protocol users.
caveat: Directness: Observational context; not intervention evidence. Limitations: Residual confounding; self-reported diet; substitution modeling; participant count not verified here; no direct protein-floor intervention. Population mismatch: Cohort populations may differ from Murph users and modern high-protein consumers.

headline: Young active adults mostly met high protein intakes through whole foods, not supplements.
implication: Use as implementation context only; it describes how active young adults consume protein but does not test health or performance outcomes.
caveat: Directness: Measurement and implementation context; no intervention. Limitations: Cross-sectional; young adults; dietary records from prior studies; no causal outcomes. Population mismatch: Young active adults may not represent older, clinical, or low-appetite users.

headline: Supplement-plus-training signals are positive but confounded by resistance training and calorie restriction.
implication: Use only as adjacent supplement-plus-training context; do not claim isolated protein-floor efficacy.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent and confounded: high protein with supplements plus resistance training under hypocaloric dieting. Limitations: Small sample; male police officers; old trial; simultaneous calorie restriction and resistance training; supplement-source comparison not cleanly isolated. Population mismatch: Overweight police officers may differ from general Murph users.

headline: Protein-increase advice in older adults changed more than protein alone.
implication: Use as implementation context for older adults: monitor total energy and macronutrient substitution when advising protein increases.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent implementation evidence in older adults, not direct protein-floor efficacy. Limitations: Secondary analysis; older low-protein sample; dietary advice rather than controlled dose delivery; outcome is intake composition. Population mismatch: Older adults with low habitual protein intake may differ from younger or already high-protein users.

headline: Self-prepared carbohydrate-reduced high-protein dieting improved markers in type 2 diabetes, but it is clinical adjacent evidence.
implication: Use only as clinical supervised adjacent evidence; carbohydrate reduction and diabetes treatment context prevent direct attribution to protein floor.
caveat: Directness: Clinical adjacent variant; not general protein-floor efficacy. Limitations: Open-label extension; small sample; no randomized comparator during extension; carbohydrate reduction cointervention; diabetes population. Population mismatch: Adults with type 2 diabetes differ from generally healthy protocol users.

headline: High animal- and plant-protein diets reduced liver/metabolic markers in type 2 diabetes, but this is clinical-context evidence.
implication: Use as clinical supervised context in type 2 diabetes; do not generalize to healthy users or infer protein-floor efficacy.
caveat: Directness: Clinical supervised adjacent evidence; not general protocol evidence. Limitations: Type 2 diabetes population; participant count and exact duration not verified here; clinical diet design; source comparison rather than protein floor. Population mismatch: People with type 2 diabetes differ from generally healthy Murph users.

headline: High-protein partial meal replacement improved weight-loss markers, but fasting added no clear advantage and micronutrients require monitoring.
implication: Use as adjacent meal-replacement context; alternate-day fasting did not clearly add advantage and micronutrient status should be monitored.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent variant: high-protein partial meal replacement and fasting, not a food-first protein floor. Limitations: Participant count not verified in extracted ledger; cointervention with meal replacements and fasting; weight-loss context; micronutrient signals require caution. Population mismatch: Weight-loss-program participants may differ from maintenance or performance users.

headline: Lean beef was compatible with short-term lipid improvements inside a low-saturated-fat diet pattern.
implication: Use as source-quality context: lean beef can fit into a low-saturated-fat cardiometabolic diet, but it is not direct evidence for a 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day target.
