caveat: Directness: Adjacent source-quality trial, not a protein-floor trial. Limitations: Small controlled-feeding sample; short periods; elevated-LDL population; protein dose not framed as g/kg/day target. Population mismatch: Adults with elevated LDL may differ from general Murph users.

headline: Soy foods appeared comparable to non-soy protein foods inside a high-protein program.
implication: Use as source-flexibility context: soy-based high-protein delivery appears comparable to non-soy in this trial, but the study is a weight-loss/maintenance design.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent: high-protein weight-loss/maintenance pattern, not a clean g/kg floor trial. Limitations: Non-inferiority design; energy-restricted/maintenance context; source-specific rather than dose-specific. Population mismatch: Adults with overweight/obesity in weight-loss care may not represent all protocol users.

headline: Soy and meat high-protein weight-loss diets looked similar over short crossover periods.
implication: Use as no-clear-advantage source-quality context: vegetarian soy and meat protein looked similar over short energy-restricted periods.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent: high-protein percent-energy weight-loss diets, not 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protocol. Limitations: Small male-only sample; very short periods; energy restriction; source comparison only. Population mismatch: Obese men in a short controlled trial differ from general free-living protocol users.

headline: Lean beef inclusion did not outperform red-meat restriction inside high-protein weight loss.
implication: Use as no-clear-source-advantage context: lean beef inclusion did not make the high-protein weight-loss program clearly better or worse in the extracted summary.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent: weight-loss high-protein pattern, not 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day maintenance target. Limitations: Energy-restricted obesity sample; source-comparison design; protein dose not isolated as the protocol floor. Population mismatch: Weight-loss participants may differ from general Murph users or performance-focused users.

headline: Protein amount may influence energy expenditure; protein type has no clear thermogenesis advantage.
implication: Use as mechanism/context: protein amount may affect expenditure, but source type does not clearly drive thermogenesis.
caveat: Directness: Mechanistic aggregate evidence; not direct protocol efficacy. Limitations: Heterogeneous trials; aggregate thermogenesis endpoints; participant counts not extracted here; not tied to 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day target. Population mismatch: Included trial populations may not match individual Murph users.

headline: OmniHeart diet-pattern paper clarifies source delivery but is not standalone efficacy evidence.
implication: Use for implementation context and artifact traceability; do not cite it as an independent efficacy result.
caveat: Directness: Measurement and implementation context for adjacent OmniHeart evidence. Limitations: Not an independent intervention outcome paper; does not isolate protein dose efficacy. Population mismatch: Controlled-feeding research environment differs from free-living protocol users.

headline: Higher beef supplementation did not clearly improve post-weight-loss maintenance outcomes.
implication: Use as no-clear-advantage source-dose context; do not infer that higher red-meat delivery improves protein-floor outcomes.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent source-dose trial after weight loss, not a protein-floor target trial. Limitations: Post-weight-loss population; beef dose comparison rather than total protein floor; short maintenance period; completer/per-protocol distinctions matter. Population mismatch: Adults after rapid weight loss may differ from weight-stable Murph users.

headline: Plant-for-animal protein substitution may modestly improve lipid markers, but it is not protein-floor efficacy evidence.
implication: Use as lipid-source context only; do not claim that plant protein substitution proves the protein-floor protocol is effective.
caveat: Directness: Same-mechanism source-substitution evidence, not direct protocol evidence. Limitations: Aggregate review of heterogeneous substitution trials; varying foods, doses, and durations; lipid endpoints rather than protocol adherence or body composition. Population mismatch: Trial populations and substitution contexts may differ from Murph users selecting protein-floor foods.

headline: Protein quality may affect muscle anabolism, but evidence is heterogeneous and often mechanistic.
implication: Use as mechanistic/source-quality context; do not convert acute MPS differences into guaranteed long-term body-composition outcomes.
caveat: Directness: Same-mechanism review; not a direct protein-floor protocol trial. Limitations: Heterogeneous acute and chronic studies; participant counts and effect sizes not extracted here; source-quality metrics vary. Population mismatch: Review includes varied populations and interventions, not one Murph protocol population.

headline: Plant-based meat alternatives improved selected biomarkers versus animal meat in a short crossover trial.
implication: Use as product/source context rather than direct protein-floor evidence; plant-based alternatives may shift some risk markers but processing and sodium should still be considered.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent source/product comparison, not a protein-dose trial. Limitations: Small sample; short phases; product-specific plant-based alternatives; not designed around 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day. Population mismatch: Healthy adults consuming provided products may differ from free-living protocol users.

headline: Higher-protein OmniHeart pattern improved cardiometabolic markers but is not a g/kg protein-floor test.
implication: Use as adjacent macronutrient-pattern evidence only: the higher-protein OmniHeart pattern was not prescribed as a g/kg/day floor and was embedded in a controlled DASH-style diet.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent: higher-protein controlled-feeding pattern, not a 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day target. Limitations: Short feeding periods; controlled food provision; percent-energy protein target; whole diet pattern changed alongside protein source. Population mismatch: Adults with elevated blood pressure, not necessarily resistance-trained or generally healthy Murph users.

headline: Protein amount showed some signals, but animal versus vegetarian source did not clearly dominate.
implication: Use as adjacent evidence: source type did not clearly dominate, but higher protein percentage during energy restriction may influence satiety and lipids.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent: percent-energy protein levels in energy-restricted diets, not a free-living g/kg floor. Limitations: Small analyzed sample; short periods; energy restriction; extracted effects are not hard outcomes. Population mismatch: Overweight/obese weight-loss participants may differ from weight-stable or athletic Murph users.

headline: Lean red meat plus exercise did not improve primary muscle or cognitive outcomes in older adults.
implication: Use as mixed/negative boundary evidence; do not imply that adding lean red meat to exercise always improves older-adult muscle outcomes.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent: source-specific protein plus exercise, not isolated protein floor. Limitations: Older adult population; exercise cointervention; source-specific red-meat prescription; primary outcomes null; some signals secondary/per-protocol. Population mismatch: Community-dwelling older adults differ from younger and athletic protocol users.

headline: Lean red meat plus resistance training improved muscle outcomes in elderly women, but the cointervention limits attribution.
implication: Use as adjacent source-delivery evidence for older women doing resistance training; do not generalize the result to protein alone or to all Murph users.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent: source-specific whole-food protein with exercise, not protein floor alone. Limitations: Cluster design; elderly women only; resistance-training cointervention; protein intake around the lower edge of the protocol target; short duration. Population mismatch: Older women in retirement villages differ from younger, male, athletic, or non-training users.

headline: Higher protein did not protect lean mass or resting metabolic rate during very-low-calorie dieting.
implication: Use as boundary evidence against overclaiming lean-mass preservation from protein alone during very-low-calorie dieting.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent safety/boundary evidence in very-low-calorie dieting; not a normal protein-floor protocol. Limitations: Severe energy restriction; total diet replacement; short duration; protein amounts may not match 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day; clinical weight-loss context. Population mismatch: VLCD participants with overweight/obesity differ from general free-living users.

headline: Meat and nonmeat sources differed on LDL-related markers under controlled feeding.
implication: Use as source-quality caveat: protein-floor recommendations should not ignore saturated fat and protein-source selection.
caveat: Directness: Same-mechanism source-quality evidence, not a total protein-floor efficacy trial. Limitations: Short feeding periods; lipid surrogate endpoints; not a g/kg target; source assignments may not reflect typical free-living diets. Population mismatch: Generally healthy adults in controlled feeding may differ from Murph users with varying lipid risk.

headline: Matched high-protein vegan and omnivorous diets supported similar muscle protein synthesis and hypertrophy in young adults.
implication: Use as source-flexibility evidence for trained or training young adults: vegan and omnivorous high-protein diets can perform similarly when total protein is matched and resistance training is present.
caveat: Directness: Adjacent-to-direct for source delivery at high protein intakes; not a protein-floor dose-response trial. Limitations: Small young-adult sample; high-volume resistance training; carefully supported diets; source comparison without low-protein control. Population mismatch: Young healthy training participants may not match older, sedentary, clinical, or weight-loss users.

headline: Low-dose whey did not preserve lean mass more than sucrose during extreme energy deficit.
implication: Use as a mismatch/context source showing that energy deficit and exercise volume can dominate outcomes; do not generalize it to the 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day floor.
caveat: Protein dose was 0.8 g/kg/day, the intervention was only four days, and the laboratory exercise/energy-deficit model is far from normal implementation.

headline: Protein-distribution commentary supports flexibility, not a direct outcome claim.
implication: Use to avoid rigid meal-frequency requirements when presenting the protein floor.
caveat: This is a response/commentary and should not be promoted as direct protocol efficacy evidence.

headline: Breakfast protein may help with muscle-mass signals, but strength and causal evidence are unclear.
implication: Use breakfast as a practical adherence option rather than a required timing rule for the protein floor.
caveat: Scoping-review evidence was heterogeneous and not limited to the Murph target-dose range.

headline: Very high protein did not improve short-term muscle-damage recovery versus moderate protein.
implication: Keep recovery claims modest; a protein floor may support adequacy, but this trial does not show acute recovery benefits from overshooting it.
caveat: The trial was small, short, and used a strenuous-exercise damage model in active older adults.

headline: In vegetarians, 2.0 g/kg/day did not outperform 1.2 g/kg/day for short-term EIMD recovery.
implication: Preserve this null result and avoid promising recovery advantages from the upper end of the floor.
caveat: This was a small young vegetarian crossover study using pea-protein supplementation and laboratory-induced muscle damage.

headline: Protein supplementation did not add clear strength or performance gains on top of resistance training in healthy older adults.
implication: Supports separating protein-floor adequacy from claims that supplementation necessarily amplifies resistance-training outcomes.
caveat: Dose, supplement type, baseline diet, and RT program varied; findings are older-adult and training-specific.

headline: Protein supplementation improved lean body mass, but timing and strength outcomes were not clearly confirmed.
implication: Supports a cautious daily-protein-first framing for body composition while keeping timing claims and strength promises bounded.
caveat: The included RCTs varied in dose, timing, participant age, and exercise context, so this is not direct evidence for the exact Murph 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day floor.

headline: Target-range protein with supervised resistance training improved body composition and performance in overweight women.
implication: Use as adjacent, cointervention-heavy support for protein-floor implementation in a training context, not as protein-only causality.
caveat: Effects cannot be separated from supervised RT, dietary counseling, energy-intake changes, and supplementation; safety follow-up was only eight weeks.

headline: Resistance-training meta-regression anchors the 1.6 g/kg/day neighborhood.
implication: Strong same-mechanism context for trained users and dose-boundary language.
caveat: Mostly supplement-plus-training evidence; not protein-floor monotherapy.

headline: Broad dose-response meta-analysis supports muscle-mass boundary framing.
implication: Useful for locating the protein floor in a diminishing-returns landscape.
caveat: Broad pooled RCTs, not a single direct Murph protocol trial.

headline: Higher protein reduced lean-mass loss in short athlete cuts.
implication: Supports lean-mass retention as an adjacent energy-deficit athlete use case.
caveat: Small, short, athlete-only and above-floor dosing; not a general maintenance protocol claim.

headline: Higher protein improved body-composition outcomes in intense exercise plus energy deficit.
implication: Supports a high-protein training-cut variant, not a general floor claim.
caveat: 2.4 g/kg/day, young men, energy deficit, and intense exercise make directness limited.

headline: Modern healthy-adult synthesis supports muscle-outcome context.
implication: Useful for general muscle-mass framing when subgroup boundaries are retained.
caveat: Not a single direct protocol; subgroup heterogeneity matters.

headline: Protein-plus-strength-training dose-response supports strength context.
implication: Useful for protocol language tying strength outcomes to training, not protein alone.
caveat: Pooled evidence; exact protocol and training exposure vary.

headline: Energy-restricted trained-athlete meta-regression is adjacent, not direct floor evidence.
implication: Useful for body-composition variant boundaries and dose-response context in dieting athletes.
caveat: Do not use as a direct protocol claim for weight-stable general users.

headline: Small novice-bodybuilder study supports adequacy boundaries, not unlimited dose escalation.
implication: Useful for cautioning that higher intakes beyond adequate may not automatically improve mass or strength.
caveat: Older, small, male-only training study.

headline: Energy-restricted high-protein diet meta-analysis is weight-loss context.
implication: Helpful for adjacent weight-loss/body-composition interpretation.
caveat: Dose form and energy restriction prevent direct floor claims.

headline: Protein supplementation plus resistance training supports muscle-adaptation context.
implication: Can inform trained-user expectations while keeping supplement/training boundaries explicit.
caveat: Not a whole-diet, nontraining protein-floor trial.

headline: Very-high-protein trained-user trial is an upper-bound comparator.
implication: Useful for separating protein-floor claims from 3+ g/kg/day bodybuilding-style protocols.
caveat: Dose far exceeds the protocol target and includes heavy training.

headline: Older-adult weight-loss factorial trial is useful but cointervention-limited.
implication: Informs older weight-loss variants and exercise separation.
caveat: Not a clean general protein-floor trial.

headline: Postmenopausal resistance-exercise RCT did not show added lean-mass gain.
implication: Keeps the protocol evidence landscape honest about subgroup/null findings.
caveat: Population-specific and not necessarily generalizable to all users.

headline: Nonfrail older-adult meta-analysis is mixed, not universally supportive.
implication: Useful for cautioning subgroup claims in older adults.
caveat: Supplement and exercise heterogeneity limits protocol specificity.

headline: Elderly protein-plus-resistance-training synthesis supports mass/strength but function is mixed.
implication: Useful for older-user variants with resistance training.
caveat: Supplement and training cointerventions; function outcomes less certain.

headline: Recent recreational-athlete dieting RCT is adjacent and needs detailed extraction before claims.
implication: Useful to flag as a separate athlete energy-restriction variant.
caveat: Sample size, dose arms, and effect estimates not extracted here.

headline: Post-hospital protein-enriched foods improved intake but not performance.
implication: Important null implementation evidence for clinical older adults.
caveat: Post-hospital population and enriched-food intervention differ from healthy-user protocol.

headline: Older-adult protein-plus-resistance-exercise synthesis informs subgroup context.
implication: Useful for aging subgroup expectations when training is present.
caveat: Supplementation and resistance-exercise cointervention limit direct protein-floor use.

headline: Female physique-athlete RCT informs specialized body-composition variants.
implication: Useful for trained female athlete contexts while not generalizing to all users.
caveat: Specialized athlete sample and training cointervention.

headline: Frail/undernourished elderly RCT is clinically important but population-mismatched.
implication: Useful for clinician-supervised frailty variants and safety boundaries.
caveat: Do not generalize to healthy users.

headline: Physically active older-adult RCT supports lean-mass context.
implication: Useful for older active-user subgroup expectations.
caveat: Supplement trial; dose and long-term safety not re-extracted.

headline: Protein-matched vegan/omnivore trial informs source delivery.
implication: Useful for implementation: plant-based users may meet target with appropriate planning/supplementation.
caveat: Not a trial of high versus low protein; young male training context.

headline: Whole-food high-protein diet plus concurrent training informs older-adult implementation.
implication: Useful for food-based, training-linked older-user variants.
caveat: Protein effect is not isolated from concurrent exercise.

headline: Senior habitual-protein RCT informs implementation boundaries.
implication: Useful for older-adult adherence and staged training variants.
caveat: Staged resistance training and senior population limit directness.

headline: Recent active-adult RCT is close but short and context-dependent.
implication: Useful for active middle-aged user context while awaiting exact dose/result extraction.
caveat: Eight weeks and no extracted effect estimates; avoid strong claims.

headline: Frail-elderly protein trial belongs to clinical/frailty context.
implication: Useful for boundary language around clinician-supervised populations.
caveat: Do not generalize clinical frailty findings to healthy adults.

headline: Lean-athlete caloric-restriction review defines a higher-dose variant boundary.
implication: Useful for separating athlete cuts from a basic floor.
caveat: Systematic review/guidance, not direct general-population evidence.

headline: Recovery-focused high-versus-moderate protein trial is adjacent.
implication: Useful for trained-user recovery endpoints if kept separate from long-term floor claims.
caveat: Short-term recovery design, not a longitudinal protein-floor efficacy trial.

headline: Habitual-intake strata in older women are context, not randomized floor proof.
implication: Useful for baseline-intake subgroup framing.
caveat: Do not infer causality from nonrandomized habitual-intake strata.

headline: Older-adult metabolic/signaling RCT is mechanistic context.
implication: May inform optional metabolic endpoints, not direct protein-floor claims.
caveat: Exact dose/effects not extracted; older adult population.

headline: Athlete intake-strata study is noncausal context.
implication: Useful for variant boundaries around 1.6-1.8 vs >2.0 g/kg/day.
caveat: Observed intake groups; confounding likely.

headline: Acute MPS dose-response is mechanism, not daily floor efficacy.
implication: Useful for meal-distribution explanations only.
caveat: Do not infer long-term body composition from acute MPS alone.

headline: Male weight-loss RCT is adjacent physical-performance context.
implication: Can inform weight-loss variants, not general maintenance claims.
caveat: Energy restriction and obesity population mismatch.

headline: Protein distribution evidence is mixed and not daily-dose proof.
implication: Useful for optional meal pacing, not protocol efficacy.
caveat: Distribution is a separate exposure from total daily dose.

headline: Proteomic RCT is mechanistic context, not protocol efficacy.
implication: Can inform biological plausibility sections only if clearly labeled.
caveat: Do not promote proteomic changes into user-facing outcome claims.

headline: Athlete narrative review is guidance context.
implication: Helpful for variant framing, not direct evidence claims.
caveat: Use primary studies for claims.

headline: Protein timing meta-analysis is implementation context.
implication: Useful for avoiding timing-vs-dose conflation.
caveat: Not direct daily-dose evidence.

headline: Arctic military field study is stress-context mechanism evidence.
implication: Useful for extreme-environment variants where energy balance dominates.
caveat: Not a civilian daily high-protein protocol.

headline: Per-meal protein review informs implementation, not efficacy.
implication: Useful for meal pacing and absorption-myth boundaries.
caveat: Narrative/mechanistic source.

headline: Track-and-field protein review is sport-specific context.
implication: Useful for athlete variant boundaries only.
caveat: Narrative review; not a protocol trial.

headline: Enhanced protein preserved muscle mass during weight loss, but not strength or physical function.
implication: Useful for body-composition monitoring during weight-loss protein-floor experiments.
caveat: Risk of bias ranged from low to high, and function outcomes were not significantly protected.

headline: Protein above the RDA favored lean mass under energy restriction or resistance training, but not in nonstressed adults.
implication: Supports stress-state boundaries for when a protein floor is likely most relevant.
caveat: Average >RDA intake was about 1.30 g/kg/day, below the full 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protocol target.

headline: Increased-protein interventions produced a modest average body-weight reduction versus controls.
implication: Adjacent support for expecting small weight-related effects if adherence and comparator diet are tracked.
caveat: Interventions were heterogeneous and commonly reported as percent energy rather than g/kg/day.

headline: Review proposes 1.2-1.6 g/kg/day and 25-30 g/meal as candidate targets but flags long-term adherence limits.
implication: Helpful for designing dose and meal-distribution targets near the protein-floor range.
caveat: Narrative review; not a primary pooled test of the Murph protein-floor protocol.

headline: Higher-protein preloads acutely increased fullness, but the source cautions against extrapolating to weight outcomes.
implication: Supports appetite/fullness measurement in a protein-floor experiment without becoming direct efficacy evidence.
caveat: Acute preload studies are not daily 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day interventions and do not establish body-weight effects.

headline: Higher protein modestly reduced weight regain in a maintenance-focused meta-analysis.
implication: Supports using weight-regain prevention as a maintenance endpoint for post-weight-loss users.
caveat: Maintenance-after-weight-loss evidence; exact g/kg protein-floor implementation requires trial-level extraction.

headline: Acute protein improved appetite and hormone markers; longer-term effects were inconclusive.
implication: Supports measuring appetite and hormone-adjacent endpoints without assuming durable appetite suppression.
caveat: Acute mechanisms may not persist in free-living daily-protein interventions.

headline: Mechanistic review links protein to satiety, energy expenditure, and fat-free mass but keeps comorbidity claims inconclusive.
implication: Useful for choosing Murph endpoints and caveating metabolic claims.
caveat: Narrative review; not a direct protocol test.

headline: Review frames protein mechanisms and flags bone, calcium, and blood-pressure considerations.
implication: Supports monitoring safety and body-composition context rather than making direct efficacy claims.
caveat: Blood-pressure caution is mechanistic/review-level and susceptible-population specific.

headline: DioGenes-centered review suggests higher protein plus lower GI helped maintenance, but protein is not isolated.
implication: Useful for ad-libitum implementation and maintenance context.
caveat: Protein and glycemic index changed together; family and post-weight-loss context limit directness.

headline: Elite-athlete review recommends 1.6-2.4 g/kg/day during weight loss but is population-specific.
implication: Useful for athlete dose-boundary context and not for general-population claims.
caveat: Elite athlete, energy-restriction, and training context are not the same as a general Murph protein-floor protocol.

headline: Expert review summarizes satiety, thermogenesis, and fat-free-mass rationale for moderately elevated protein.
implication: Background rationale only; useful for source-chaining and endpoint framing.
caveat: No standardized g/kg/day protocol or pooled effect estimate.

headline: Macronutrient appetite review supports measurement caution for satiety and intake endpoints.
implication: Use to design appetite and energy-intake measurement, not to claim protein-floor efficacy.
caveat: Broad macronutrient review, not a protein intervention synthesis.

headline: Registry context for protein distribution physiology, not daily protein-floor efficacy
implication: Use for measurement and mechanism context when separating total daily protein from meal distribution.
caveat: No registry results are posted and the registry record does not state a clean 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day target.

headline: DiOGenes registry is publication-linkage and design context
implication: Use to map DiOGenes protocol arms and linked publications before citing any publication-specific result.
caveat: Registry has no posted results and does not state a 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day protein prescription.

headline: Adjacent high-dose protein plus intense-training registry context
implication: Useful for noting that high-protein targets have been studied under severe supervised energy deficit and intense training, not as a simple floor protocol.
caveat: The tested high-protein dose was 2.4 g/kg/day and the cointervention was intense exercise 6 days/week.

headline: Lower-dose high-protein meal-replacement registry context
implication: Use to document a clinical high- versus standard-protein weight-loss design and its linked publication.
caveat: The registry high-protein target is 1.34 g/kg/day, below the protocol target, and no registry results are posted.

headline: Older-adult higher-protein weight-loss registry results are adjacent and mixed
implication: Use as supervised older-adult weight-loss and safety context, especially for function, lean mass, and adverse-event monitoring.
caveat: Dose target was ≥1.0 g/kg/day and bundled with a 1200 kcal meal-replacement weight-loss plan, so it is not direct evidence for a 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day floor.

headline: Acute metabolic-chamber context for high-protein total diet replacement
implication: Use to frame possible acute energy-expenditure, substrate-balance, appetite, and blood-marker signals.
caveat: This is an acute 32-hour inpatient product-based crossover record in healthy young women, not long-term protein-floor outcome evidence.

headline: Acute men's metabolic-chamber context for high-protein total diet replacement
implication: Use to define mechanistic endpoints such as energy expenditure, fat balance, appetite, and urine nitrogen.
caveat: Short duration, product-based feeding, healthy male sample, and no registry results prevent direct protocol claims.

headline: Supervised older-adult 1.5 g/kg/day registry design without posted results
implication: Useful for endpoint selection and older-adult safety/adherence boundaries when considering 1.5 g/kg/day targets.
caveat: Registry status is unknown and no outcome results are posted.

headline: Named-diet registry context, not a protein-dose trial
implication: Use as a boundary record showing why named low-carb/high-protein diets should not be promoted as direct protein-floor evidence.
caveat: No achieved protein dose or registry results are posted.
